stories.headline: ‘Arnab’ packs rain, not cyclone strength: Kolkata remains under weather alert
stories.title: ‘Arnab’ packs rain, not cyclone strength: Kolkata remains under weather alert
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: ‘Cyclone Arnab’ is officially a deep depression, but heavy rain, thunderstorms and gusty winds continue to threaten Bengal.
The word ‘cyclone’ may have been dominating social media feeds, but the India Meteorological Department has drawn a clear line: the system being referred to as ‘Arnab’ is not a cyclone.
It is a deep depression, and Kolkata still has plenty of rain to contend with.
The weather system over the Bay of Bengal has brought heavy rain, thunderstorms and gusty winds across parts of Bengal, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.
But despite the growing public attention around it, the system has not attained the wind speed required for classification as a cyclonic storm.
The deep depression currently has maximum sustained winds of 55-65 kmph, with gusts reaching 75 kmph.
Under the IMD's classification, a deep depression has an average wind speed of 50-61 kmph, while a cyclonic storm requires wind speeds of 62-88 kmph.
That distinction matters because the system widely being described online as “Cyclone Arnab” does not officially qualify for the cyclone tag.
According to the IMD, the deep depression over the north Andhra Pradesh coast moved slowly west-northwestwards at around 3 kmph at 6 am.
It crossed the coast close to southwest of Kalingapatnam between 11 pm on September 23 and 1 am on September 24, carrying maximum sustained winds of 55-65 kmph and gusts of up to 75 kmph.
The system subsequently moved west-northwestwards and was located over north coastal Andhra Pradesh.
It was around 50 km west of Kalingapatnam, 80 km north-northeast of Visakhapatnam and 170 km southwest of Gopalpur in Odisha.

stories.headline: Flood alert sounded in North Andhra as rivers swell
stories.title: Flood alert sounded in North Andhra as rivers swell
stories.summary: With more rain forecast over the next few days, officials have deployed NDRF and SDRF teams at sensitive places to take up relief measures, river-level monitoring intensified and residents from vulnerable low-lying areas being shifted
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Srikakulam and Vizianagaram district administrations have been placed on high alert as the Nagavali, Vamsadhara, Suvarnamukhi, Jhanjavati, Vegavathi and other rivers received huge inflows in their catchment areas following the impact of the deep depression that crossed Kalingapatnam sea coast in Srikakulam district in the early hours of Thursday.
Srikakulam Collector Swapnil Dinakar Pundkar said: “Irrigation officials issued the first flood warning for the Vamsadhara and Nagavali Rivers.”
He said that the situation was under control despite the heavy rains and strong winds, which reached speeds of around 55kmph as the depression crossed the coast.
“We will effectively handle any eventuality as officials of all departments are working in tandem.
NDRF and SDRF teams have been kept ready at sensitive places to take up relief measures.
People living in low lying areas are being shifted to safe places, “ Mr. Swapnil told.
The Hindu.
Vizianagaram Collector S. Ramsundar Reddy visited Bhogapuram, Pusapatirega and other areas close to the sea coast to monitor the situation.
He said: “The district will witness heavy downpour for the next couple of days with the impact of the cyclone as per the bulletin of Indian Meteorological Department.
Flood situation in the rivers will be monitored on an hourly basis.
Relief measures will be taken up for people living in low lying areas.”
The Parvatipuram -Manyam district administration has set up control rooms in all mandals to oversee relief measures.

stories.headline: Karnataka CM, Dy. CM demand Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, seek fresh roll revision
stories.title: Karnataka CM, Dy. CM demand Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, seek fresh roll revision
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Seeking the immediate resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar demanded that the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls be withdrawn, followed by a fresh revision.

Mr. Shivakumar said the issue concerned the voting rights of every citizen and that it was not about any political party, arguing that the SIR had been conducted in a manner that could affect citizens.
He said similar concerns had emerged in West Bengal, Bihar and other States.
Karnataka, too, was now facing the same situation, he said, adding that he had sought more time from the Election Commission of India (ECI).

Questioning the functioning of the poll panel, Mr. Shivakumar pointed to differences among its members, with two Election Commissioners raising objections to major decisions, including changes to Form 6 and the ECI’s software.
He said decisions should not be imposed when a majority did not agree with an opinion.
“In such a situation, the Chief Election Commissioner should voluntarily resign on moral grounds,” he said.

Further questioning the manner in which Forms 6, 7 and 8 were being used during the revision, Mr. Shivakumar said the process needed wider scrutiny and argued that the issue should be discussed extensively, including in Parliament.

Referring to the “vote chori” concerns raised by Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi in the Mahadevapura and Aland Assembly constituencies, and allegations of duplicate voters in Haryana, Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara sought an independent inquiry into the functioning of the ECI and demanded the removal of the CEC.

Dr. Parameshwara questioned whether the three-member constitutional body was functioning through collective decision-making when two of its members had raised objections to decisions being issued without their approval.
“Has a three-member constitutional body been reduced to the will of one individual, Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar?
He is first among equals, not above the Commission,” he said, arguing that the majority view could not be bypassed.

stories.headline: Syndicate member criticises union election reforms in Calicut varsity
stories.title: Syndicate member criticises union election reforms in Calicut varsity
stories.summary: Panel report on proposed election rule reforms was presented as an “out-of-agenda” item without prior circulation to members, says the member
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A pro-Left Syndicate member in the University of Calicut has claimed that the proposal to revamp the rules related to college union election was approved at a recent meeting without detailed discussions.

K. Mohamed Haneefa, the Syndicate member, said in a statement on Thursday (September 24, 2026) that the report of a panel that studied the proposed reforms to the election rules was presented as an “out-of-agenda” item without being circulated to members in advance.
The report was objected to by some members who sought adequate time for examination and discussion, he said.
Mr. Haneefa also criticised the move to form a Calicut University Research Scholars’ Union for all full-time PhD research scholars.

He said that more clarity was required on how their academic and social links with the student community of the host institution would be maintained while they were being brought under a separate university-level union.

The geographical distribution of research scholars across the university campus and affiliated colleges also should be considered while designing a representative structure that can ensure effective participation and communication, he added.

stories.headline: How Ather’s foray into mass market pits it against giant incumbents TVS, Bajaj
stories.title: How Ather’s foray into mass market pits it against giant incumbents TVS, Bajaj
stories.summary: Dressed in a black tee and blue jeans, Tarun Mehta walked across the stage in a hall packed with nearly 5,000 people. The co-founder and CEO of Ather Energy had run through the sequence the day before—where to pause, where to slow down and where to let a joke land. It also had him pretending to be a regular office commuter with a laptop bag and a lunchbox in his hands who opens the luggage space of his scooter with a tap of the knee.But dry runs do not prepare you fully for a roomful of enthusiasts. Every time a new feature of the Konarc, Ather’s newest scooter, flashed on the giant screen behind Mehta, the hall erupted in cheers, screams and whistles, occasionally leaving him wondering what it was that clicked.The big picture of Ather’s journey since it started in 2013 holds no such riddles for Mehta. Others might question, as they did back then, why he and his co-founder Swapnil Jain were not doing ecommerce [every other Indian startup was] and, instead, choosing deeptech hardware.Those doubts would be silenced by the cheers arising from that hall in Bengaluru on August 29. It was Ather Community Day, an annual gathering the Bengaluru-based company has held since 2016 when it had no product. A grand total of 30 people attended it that year. Ten years and three products later, the event pulled in 5,000.The cheers Mehta relishes more will be outside that hall, in the rough and tumble of the two-wheeler market. Konarc is Ather’s first e-scooter to be priced below ₹1 lakh, a whole ₹1 below the psychological threshold. So far, its cheapest was the Rizta, whose pricing started at ₹121,999. Both prices are without its software pack, which ranges between ₹8,500 and ₹23,500.The Konarc takes Ather headlong into a rivalry with TVS and Bajaj, two of the four—Hero MotoCorp and Honda Motorcycle and Scooter India (HMSI) are the other two—that have dominated India’s two-wheeler market for decades and flexed their distribution muscle and strong balance sheets to rise to the top in electric two-wheelers. The mass market is where consumers come less for tech and features and more for the everyday reliability that the legacy guys have proven to be good at.About half the e-scooter market is in the ₹1-1.25 lakh price range. With the new scooter, Ather has a product for 90 percent of the market, claims Mehta.That also means this segment has 100 percent attention from everyone.While this battle plays out as a challenger takes on incumbents in a new playground, its outcome will signal whether a new era of two-wheeler leadership in India is on the anvil. Not only did Ather tear up the Indian startup rule book by going into deeptech hardware, it also refused to follow the rules of the two-wheeler industry.India’s automotive history, two- and four-wheelers alike, was built by companies that thrived in partnerships with multinationals in their early years. Ather is doing it on its own, obsessing over product in an industry focussed on functionality instead of making the best products in the world.The focus on functionality is best embodied by the seven decades of scooters in India. It has always been the thing that takes you from point A to B. It did not need to have a touchscreen dashboard or alerts about the next pothole. It did not need to tell you cricket match scores or send an SOS to your emergency contacts. Yet, these are the things you get when you buy an Ather and opt for its paid software platform, AtherStack Pro. It is not just the whim of a couple of tech bros. Nine out of 10 Ather buyers opt for the software bundle. “You have to bring out features that make sense at a cost that makes sense [and the customer will pay for it],” says co-founder Jain.As if that was not enough of a challenge, Ather decided to design, engineer and manufacture the entire product in-house, including the battery pack, motor, software platform and charging network. This marked it apart in the crowd of Indian startups that flooded the electric two-wheeler market relying on imports from China and making news for the wrong reasons, including getting into a kerfuffle with the government for their questionable claims to subsidy. Some of them are out, some on their way out.In contrast, Ather has nearly half its people working in research and development, unheard of in an Indian company of its size.A new two-wheeler order?This is hardly a David versus two Goliaths. In Ather’s corner is Hero MotoCorp, the world’s largest two-wheeler maker and its largest shareholder which in August increased its equity in the startup from 29.9 percent to 32.8 percent by infusing another ₹1,758 crore.Harshavardhan Chitale, Hero MotoCorp’s CEO, says this shows conviction in the long-term potential of electric mobility in India. “Importantly, this investment is complementary to, and does not diminish, our commitment to Vida.” Vida is Hero’s own electric two-wheeler brand.Ather has turned in profits on the basis of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortisation (Ebitda)—a widely followed metric for the financial health of a company. Clearly, the unusual bets are paying off.“We believed a strong premiumising market will allow the creation of strong product brands, brands that will build great experiences, like what Apple has done,” says Mehta.Electric was a new powertrain when Ather embraced it. There was no local supply chain and no one who had done it before to learn from. Ather had to develop the manufacturing process along with the product, says Sanjeev Kumar Singh, its chief operating officer.The manufacturing process is feeling the pangs to scale up. With the US-Iran war adding to the volatility in fuel prices, more consumers are veering towards electric. “When we were at 23,000 a month in January, we thought we will have 50 percent growth over the next 12 months. It came in three months. We have now hit a capacity constraint, and things will not change because the demand far exceeds what we can produce,” says Mehta.Also Read: Ather enters mass EV market, now targets 90% of India’s e scooter segmentIn August, Ather’s retail sales rose by 50 percent, behind the industry (67 percent), behind TVS (90 percent) and behind Bajaj (235 percent). Naturally, Ather is losing share in a growing market. TVS is the largest electric two-wheeler maker, with a 26.7 percent share of the market as of August. Bajaj is second with 22.4 percent. Ather’s share, 18.4 percent in March, has slipped to 15.7 percent.Mehta maintains there is demand for nearly 15,000 of its scooters every month that it is not able to meet. Its current annual capacity is 420,000. There is a new factory with an initial capacity of 500,000 a year which is likely to start churning out e-scooters by the end of this year. The second phase, as planned, will add another 500,000 a year.Rising stakes, higher gambitsAther was the first two-wheeler company in the world to put a touchscreen on the dashboard—no small feat in the Indian weather—and integrate Google Maps into it. The 450, which the company calls the “bike of scooters”, was the fastest accelerating made-in-India scooter at the time of its launch in 2018.Bikash Jyoti Biswas, Ather’s first employee and now its head of design, says the idea is to be differentiated. That differentiation pays off. Fourteen percent of Ather’s revenue now comes from the non-vehicle segment, largely its software, similar to premium motorcycle maker Royal Enfield’s.Ather designed its own charging connector, since adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards as the national standard. It runs Ather Grid, a network of more than 6,100 fast chargers in 370 cities, the largest fast-charging network for two-wheelers in India.That said, the stakes have risen to their highest level ever. The scooter Mehta launched that sunny August morning is built on a new platform and is the first true mass market product that was meant to be such. It uses a steel unibody chassis and has a metal body, a construction more commonly seen in conventional scooters. Ather’s earlier products use aluminium frame architecture and plastic body panels.Changes like these allow Ather to have better margins on the Konarc, and take the fight to TVS and Bajaj. The founders, both of them 37 this year, expect the base variant to sell the most.Also Read: TVS Motor to ramp up EV capacity by up to 25 percent by year-endBattle criesOhers are not resting on their oars.TVS and Bajaj Auto are increasing their electric vehicle capacities by at least 25 percent. One of their biggest strengths is the thriving ICE (internal combustion engine) two-wheeler business, which yields cash with generosity and gives them the ammunition to fight the electric battle with strong bulwarks.HMSI has so far failed to replicate its ICE success in electric. But it is not blind to the opportunity. “Some day Honda will get serious about electric and, with its dealer network, it can take away a large chunk of the market in no time,” says Deepesh Rathore, founder of consultancy firm InsightEV.Then there are the other startups in the fray. Simple Energy, Greaves Electric Mobility, BGauss and River Mobility have all raised money this year.The biggest fundraise was by Yamaha-backed River Mobility, a Bengaluru company that raised $120 million in August and is setting up a new plant whose capacity will be seven to eight times the current factory’s 120,000.It is preparing to come after the same customers as Ather.River has a 3 percent market share with only one scooter, the Indie, which is priced at ₹1.56 lakh. That Yamaha—a company known for quality—is comfortable selling a scooter made by River under its own name as the EC-06 says something about how seriously the Japanese company takes River’s manufacturing.“We are looking at a 7 to 10 percent market share by March 2028,” says River’s co-founder and CEO Aravind Mani. He expects the company to be Ebitda-positive once it sells about 25,000 vehicles a month, a milestone he hopes to reach by FY29.Ultraviolette Automotive, a high-performance electric motorcycle brand in which TVS has invested, is coming for Ather’s performance scooter market share. It is likely to launch its first scooter, the Tesseract, early next year which, it claims, will hit 125 kmph, well past the 90 kmph top speed of Ather’s 450X. It, too, is building a new plant, with a capacity of 250,000 a year to start with, and expandable to 500,000.“We see baseline demand for the Tesseract at 10,000 units a month. Production can begin at our existing facility and scale from there, with dedicated lines for the scooter,” says Narayan Subramaniam, co-founder and CEO of Ultraviolette.The Bengaluru-based company has been gross-margin-positive since its first day of sales, a milestone that took Ather three years to reach after its first scooter rolled off the line. Exports are 15 percent of its sales, with Europe its largest overseas market.Finally, there is friendly fire. Hero, Ather’s largest shareholder, entered the category late—in 2022—and has since climbed to fourth place in the market. TVS Motor, Bajaj Auto, Ola Electric and HMSI did not reply to Forbes India’s requests for comment.As the battle lines are drawn, Ather has to protect its identity. How will it negotiate the transition from a brand built on premium products riding on technology and features to one selling to people who simply need a scooter?Mehta believes the AtherStack Pro separation—the software bundle has to be bought separately for access to most features—helps the company maintain a higher premium than by just bundling it all together. “See, when you walk into a showroom, you don’t know how to value all these new features, including the safety features,” he says. “So, we price the basic product without the software and then let the person take the test ride and then maybe fall in love with it and eventually pay more.”Inevitably, the thinking goes back to where it all began. Premium. Technology. Features. And a couple of product-obsessed folks taking on the empire.

India’s automotive history, two- and four-wheelers alike, was built by companies that thrived in partnerships with multinationals in their early years.
Ather is doing it on its own, obsessing over product in an industry focussed on functionality instead of making the best products in the world.
The focus on functionality is best embodied by the seven decades of scooters in India.
It has always been the thing that takes you from point.
A to B. It did not need to have a touchscreen dashboard or alerts about the next pothole.
It did not need to tell you cricket match scores or send an SOS to your emergency contacts.
Yet, these are the things you get when you buy an Ather and opt for its paid software platform, AtherStack Pro.
It is not just the whim of a couple of tech bros.
Nine out of 10 Ather buyers opt for the software bundle.
“You have to bring out features that make sense at a cost that makes sense [and the customer will pay for it],” says co-founder Jain.
As if that was not enough of a challenge, Ather decided to design, engineer and manufacture the entire product in-house, including the battery pack, motor, software platform and charging network.

This marked it apart in the crowd of Indian startups that flooded the electric two-wheeler market relying on imports from China and making news for the wrong reasons, including getting into a kerfuffle with the government for their questionable claims to subsidy.
Some of them are out, some on their way out.
In contrast, Ather has nearly half its people working in research and development, unheard of in an Indian company of its size.
A new two-wheeler order?
This is hardly a David versus two Goliaths.

In Ather’s corner is Hero MotoCorp, the world’s largest two-wheeler maker and its largest shareholder which in August increased its equity in the startup from 29.9 percent to 32.8 percent by infusing another ₹1,758 crore.
Harshavardhan Chitale, Hero Moto.
Corp’s CEO, says this shows conviction in the long-term potential of electric mobility in India.
“Importantly, this investment is complementary to, and does not diminish, our commitment to Vida.” Vida is Hero’s own electric two-wheeler brand.
Ather has turned in profits on the basis of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortisation (Ebitda)—a widely followed metric for the financial health of a company.
Clearly, the unusual bets are paying off.
“We believed a strong premiumising market will allow the creation of strong product brands, brands that will build great experiences, like what Apple has done,” says Mehta.
Electric was a new powertrain when Ather embraced it.
There was no local supply chain and no one who had done it before to learn from.
Ather had to develop the manufacturing process along with the product, says Sanjeev Kumar Singh, its chief operating officer.
The manufacturing process is feeling the pangs to scale up.
With the US-Iran war adding to the volatility in fuel prices, more consumers are veering towards electric.
“When we were at 23,000 a month in January, we thought we will have 50 percent growth over the next 12 months.
It came in three months.
We have now hit a capacity constraint, and things will not change because the demand far exceeds what we can produce,” says Mehta.
Naturally, Ather is losing share in a growing market.
Bajaj is second with 22.4 percent.
Mehta maintains there is demand for nearly 15,000 of its scooters every month that it is not able to meet.
Its current annual capacity is 420,000.
There is a new factory with an initial capacity of 500,000 a year which is likely to start churning out e-scooters by the end of this year.
The second phase, as planned, will add another 500,000 a year.
Rising stakes, higher gambitsAther was the first two-wheeler company in the world to put a touchscreen on the dashboard—no small feat in the Indian weather—and integrate Google Maps into it.
The 450, which the company calls the “bike of scooters”, was the fastest accelerating made-in-India scooter at the time of its launch in 2018.
Bikash Jyoti Biswas, Ather’s first employee and now its head of design, says the idea is to be differentiated.
That differentiation pays off.
Fourteen percent of Ather’s revenue now comes from the non-vehicle segment, largely its software, similar to premium motorcycle maker Royal Enfield’s.
Ather designed its own charging connector, since adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards as the national standard.
It runs Ather Grid, a network of more than 6,100 fast chargers in 370 cities, the largest fast-charging network for two-wheelers in India.
That said, the stakes have risen to their highest level ever.
The scooter Mehta launched that sunny August morning is built on a new platform and is the first true mass market product that was meant to be such.
It uses a steel unibody chassis and has a metal body, a construction more commonly seen in conventional scooters.
Ather’s earlier products use aluminium frame architecture and plastic body panels.
Changes like these allow Ather to have better margins on the Konarc, and take the fight to TVS and Bajaj.
The founders, both of them 37 this year, expect the base variant to sell the most.
Battle criesOhers are not resting on their oars.

One of their biggest strengths is the thriving ICE (internal combustion engine) two-wheeler business, which yields cash with generosity and gives them the ammunition to fight the electric battle with strong bulwarks.
HMSI has so far failed to replicate its ICE success in electric.
But it is not blind to the opportunity.
“Some day Honda will get serious about electric and, with its dealer network, it can take away a large chunk of the market in no time,” says Deepesh Rathore, founder of consultancy firm InsightEV.
Then there are the other startups in the fray.
Simple Energy, Greaves Electric Mobility, BGauss and River Mobility have all raised money this year.

The biggest fundraise was by Yamaha-backed River Mobility, a Bengaluru company that raised $120 million in August and is setting up a new plant whose capacity will be seven to eight times the current factory’s 120,000.
It is preparing to come after the same customers as Ather.

That Yamaha—a company known for quality—is comfortable selling a scooter made by River under its own name as the EC-06 says something about how seriously the Japanese company takes River’s manufacturing.
He expects the company to be Ebitda-positive once it sells about 25,000 vehicles a month, a milestone he hopes to reach by FY29.
Ultraviolette Automotive, a high-performance electric motorcycle brand in which TVS has invested, is coming for Ather’s performance scooter market share.

It is likely to launch its first scooter, the Tesseract, early next year which, it claims, will hit 125 kmph, well past the 90 kmph top speed of Ather’s 450X. It, too, is building a new plant, with a capacity of 250,000 a year to start with, and expandable to 500,000.
“We see baseline demand for the Tesseract at 10,000 units a month.
Production can begin at our existing facility and scale from there, with dedicated lines for the scooter,” says Narayan Subramaniam, co-founder and CEO of Ultraviolette.
The Bengaluru-based company has been gross-margin-positive since its first day of sales, a milestone that took Ather three years to reach after its first scooter rolled off the line.
Finally, there is friendly fire.
Hero, Ather’s largest shareholder, entered the category late—in 2022—and has since climbed to fourth place in the market.
TVS Motor, Bajaj Auto, Ola Electric and HMSI did not reply to Forbes India’s requests for comment.
As the battle lines are drawn, Ather has to protect its identity.
How will it negotiate the transition from a brand built on premium products riding on technology and features to one selling to people who simply need a scooter?

Mehta believes the AtherStack Pro separation—the software bundle has to be bought separately for access to most features—helps the company maintain a higher premium than by just bundling it all together.
“See, when you walk into a showroom, you don’t know how to value all these new features, including the safety features,” he says.

“So, we price the basic product without the software and then let the person take the test ride and then maybe fall in love with it and eventually pay more.” Inevitably, the thinking goes back to where it all began.
Premium.
Technology.
Features.
And a couple of product-obsessed folks taking on the empire.

article_sentences: Tata Sons has defended its board's decision to reappoint chairman N. Chandrasekaran for five years, writing to Tata Trusts chair Noel Tata that the decision followed relevant laws and company rules.

In a letter dated 24 September addressed to Noel and signed by Tata Sons group company secretary Suprakash Mukhopadhyay, Tata Sons said it had sought legal advice from Sudipto Sarkar before the board meeting on 17 September, and later received separate legal opinions from former Chief Justice of India U.U. Lalit and former Supreme Court judge B.N. Srikrishna.

“The board, by a majority resolution, has validly resolved to reappoint Mr N Chandrasekaran as the chairman upon the expiry of his existing tenure,” said Tata Sons in its letter, according to an executive who saw it.
Mukhopadhyay’s letter responded to Noel’s two letters, dated 18 September, in which the Tata Trusts chair questioned the legality of Chandrasekaran's reappointment.
On 17 September, the Tata Sons board went against its main shareholder, Tata Trusts, in a rare case in corporate India where a company’s board disagreed with its controlling shareholder.
Tata Trusts nominees Noel and Venu Srinivasan cast opposing votes; Harish Manwani, who led the process, cast the deciding vote in favour of the reappointment, defeating Noel.
In its letter, Tata Sons explained that an independent director’s decision to break the tie on the reappointment followed legal advice from three respected legal experts.
Tata Trusts disagrees, saying that under Article 121 of Tata Sons’ rules, only a majority vote of the Trustees can approve a chairman’s reappointment.
Tata Trusts said there was no tie after its two trustees voted differently on the chairman’s reappointment.
“A casting vote cannot revive a stillborn resolution,” said Tata Trusts.
Tata Sons’ reply also included an 11-page legal opinion from Justice Lalit and an eight-page opinion from Srikrishna, according to an executive familiar with the development.
Emails sent to Tata Sons and Tata Trusts seeking comment went unanswered.

New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Thursday witnessed detailed arguments over the process adopted for the selection of Odisha’s regular Director General of Police (DGP), with the hearing focusing on the withholding of senior IPS officer Sushant Kumar Nath’s Integrity Certificate, the “Zone of Consideration” sent to the UPSC, the eligibility of Level-16 officers and the creation of Ex-Cadre DGP posts.

Nath’s Integrity Certificate issued on May 14 was based on the PARs and service records available at that time while fresh information was received from the CBI on August 4 in the Sl recruitment investigation.
The CBI said Nath “may be required to be examined.”
UPSC asked the State whether the certificate’s status had been reconsidered.
The State re-examined the records of all 11 eligible officers, withheld Nath’s certificate and sent a revised proposal with the certificates of the remaining 10 officers.
The State said it would not have been appropriate to withhold later developments from the UPSC and maintained that transparency was necessary.
On the other hand, Justice Joymalya Bagchi questioned whether withholding the Integrity Certificate on the basis of an ongoing investigation amounted to going too far.
He asked if such a step effectively placed Nath in the category of an accused.
The judge clarified that the Court was not, at this stage, attributing mala fides to the State.
He observed that an investigation is a fact-finding process and may either reveal a person’s involvement or clear that person.

stories.summary: Finally, it’s a done deal. Listing of shares of National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) on Indian bourses marks the end of a long haul and wait for investors after years of regulatory hurdle. However, NSE’s stock markets debut lacked investor euphoria. On Thursday, it was listed at Rs1,800 on the BSE, merely 1 percent premium over its issue price of Rs1,785 per share.While the Rs22,568.94 crore issue ranks NSE as India's second largest initial public offering (IPO), its larger significance lies in the culmination of one of the country's longest-running and closely watched listing sagas. The exchange's IPO plans were stalled for years amid regulatory concerns and governance issues. The listing also provides investors a direct stake in the country's dominant equity and derivatives trading platform.NSE's path to the public markets has been rather rough. It had first filed for an IPO for nearly Rs10,000-crore offer-for-sale (OFS) in 2016. However, its listing ambitions were put on hold after markets regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi), had asked NSE to withdraw the application amid compliance and governance concerns stemming from the co-location scandal. It suffered another setback in April 2019 when Sebi barred NSE from the securities markets for six months in connection with the co-location controversy.Also Read: The NSE paradox: Why market dominance may be a liabilityThe co-location controversy refers to allegations that certain brokers received preferential access to the exchange's trading systems through its co-location facility, giving them a speed advantage in executing trades. After years of regulatory scrutiny, litigations and appeals, NSE subsequently sought to resolve the matter through Sebi's settlement mechanism, agreeing to pay Rs1,491 crore to settle the co-location and related dark-fibre cases, removing a key regulatory overhang ahead of its IPO.Investors’ appetite for NSEThe issue with a price band of Rs1,700-1,785 per share was overall subscribed nearly six times with institutional investors bidding at 12.68 times and retail investors 1.4 times. The three-day sale which ended on September 21 was a pure OFS. It had already raised Rs6,746.2 crore from anchor investors, including Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), GIC Singapore, Fidelity and Societe Generale, among others.According to analysts at Bajaj Financial Securities, NSE’s continued expansion across asset classes and financial products may support further business development, while trading volumes and transaction activity remain key variables. “At the upper price band, NSE is valued at 42.9 times price-to-earnings (PE),” they say.The sheer size of the NSE IPO did little to deter investors. The NSE IPO attracted bids worth more than Rs90,000 crore, the highest ever for a public issue in India. Despite its size, the offering drew strong investor interest, making it the most subscribed among India's five largest IPOs. In comparison, Hyundai Motor India's Rs27,859-crore IPO, the country's largest public issue, was subscribed 2.3 times when it had hit the market in 2024.For perspective, LIC's Rs20,557.23-crore IPO was subscribed nearly 3 times, Paytm parent One 97 Communications' Rs18,300-crore offering received bids for 1.9 times the shares on offer and Tata Capital's Rs15,511.87-crore IPO was subscribed 1.95 times.Also Read: Ashishkumar Chauhan: The man who built NSE, and came back to rebuild trustMarket monopolyNSE is a market leader with a monopoly in cash equities, equity futures, equity options, exchange traded currency futures and exchange-traded currency options. NSE has been the largest stock exchange in India in terms of total turnover in cash market and total turnover in equity derivatives from FY2001 (from June 2000) to FY26, according to a report by Redseer Strategy Consultants. Globally, for seven consecutive years, it is at the top spot in equity derivatives contracts traded.Cash market average daily turnover (ADTO) saw strong growth between FY14 and FY26, rising from Rs13,300 crore to Rs1.1 lakh crore, reflecting deeper market penetration and increased investor participation. Retail investors have surged with increase in mobile-based trading, while co-location along with an increase in algo-trading is a noticeable trend in this segment, highlighting participation of institutional investors and traders.As of FY26, NSE commands 92.99 percent market share in cash equities based on total turnover, 99.79 percent in equity futures (based on total turnover), 74.71 percent in equity options (based on premium turnover), 99.48 percent in exchange traded currency futures (based on total turnover) and 100 percent for exchange-traded currency options (based on total industry premium turnover) in India.In FY26, NSE recorded the highest operating Ebitda margin (66.85 percent) and one of the highest net profit margins (50.98 percent of total income) among global listed exchanges. NSE's revenue from operations grew at a 5.98 percent CAGR to Rs16,601.3 crore in FY26 from Rs14,780 crore in FY24, while profit for the year grew at 11.37 percent CAGR to Rs10,302 crore from Rs8,305.74 crore over the same period.Also Read: Ashishkumar Chauhan on how NSE became a model of resilienceThe concentration riskNSE relies heavily on derivatives revenues at a time when regulators are re-examining the social and financial costs of speculative trading. The market regulator’s move to curb excessive speculation in derivatives, NSE's greatest revenue engine, could increasingly become risky.The derivative segment has seen multiple regulatory changes from the second half of FY25, especially in the derivatives market, as regulators are focussed on protecting retail investors. Average daily trading volume (ADTV) in equity futures declined to Rs159,443.21 crore in FY26 from Rs185,901.44 crore in FY25, and equity options ADTV (premium) to Rs57,661.75 crore from Rs62,448.66 crore in the same time period.NSE’s revenues are intrinsically tied to volume and value of transactions, number of new listings and breadth of investor participation. In FY26, trading services accounted for 78.65 percent of revenue from operations. From FY23 to FY25, NSE’s total revenue grew at a CAGR of 23 percent, positioning it among the top three listed exchanges globally in terms of two-year total revenue growth, according to the Redseer report.“Transaction charges formed 78.6 percent of FY26 operating revenue, including 60.2 percent from options, exposing earnings to regulatory changes, competition, pricing pressure and weaker market activity,” says Vishal Narnolia, analyst, ICICI Securities.Dependence on transaction charges for revenue indicates higher sensitivity to market volumes and trading cycles. In contrast, global peers like Intercontinental Exchange, NASDAQ, London Stock Exchange, Japan Exchange Group and Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing have diversified revenue streams, which result in a more stable earning profile compared to volume-driven Indian exchanges.NSE continues to face legacy regulatory and legal matters whose outcomes create reputational, operational and financial overhang. Besides the co-location case, there are few pending litigations.“Separately, MSEI’s Rs857 crore compensation claim remains stayed by the Supreme Court, while NSE Clearing is contesting a Rs395 crore tax demand principally relating to Core SGF deductions. Adverse outcomes or additional regulatory proceedings could result in financial liabilities, operational restrictions and reputational consequences,” says Narnolia.

article_sentences: The Kerala High Court recently held that an investigating officer can be appointed as a prosecutor in a court-martial case as per the Navy (Discipline and Miscellaneous Provisions) Regulations, 1965, and that it would not violate the accused person’s fundamental right to a fair trial.

The Division Bench of Justices K. Natarajan and Johnson John held that a combined analysis of the Constitution of India, the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the Navy Act, 1957 and the Navy Regulations would indicate that, in matters of the armed forces, there are restrictions imposed on the fundamental rights of military personnel.
In such cases, the prosecutor and the investigating officer in a court-martial case could be competent witnesses.
The court inferred that even if the investigating officer is appointed as the prosecutor, he could be examined as a witness.
The petitioner was a Navy personnel with 31 years of service, undergoing a trial where he was charged with offences, including cheating.

He had previously approached a Single Bench of the court, alleging that he was denied the right to a free and fair trial, as the trial was being conducted by the prosecutor, who had also been the investigating officer of the charges levelled against him.
He claimed that he was denied access to material documents and adequate opportunities to defend the case.

He sought directions to declare the provision allowing a court-martial prosecutor to testify as a competent witness as unconstitutional, as it allegedly violated the right to a fair trial of the accused person.
The Single Judge upheld the constitutionality of the challenged regulation.

However, it held that the right to a fair trial would be infringed when the same investigating officer assumes the prosecutor role and directed the petitioner to approach the Armed Forces Tribunal for its assessment on whether the trial conducted by the prosecutor was vitiated.
The petitioner then challenged the regulation before the Division Bench.

The Central government countered the petitioner’s arguments, stating that the provisions of the Navy Act stated that fundamental rights could be modified with regard to persons who are subject to the naval law.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court today commuted the death sentence imposed on a man convicted for raping and murdering his six-year-old step-daughter in Madhya Pradesh.
A bench of Justice Vikram Nath, Justice Sandeep Mehta and Justice Vijay Bishnoi upheld his conviction but commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment.

The appellant, one Waris, was convicted by the Special Court under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, Jaora, on December 17, 2018, under Sections 376(2)(F), 376(2)(N), 376(AB), 302 and 201 of the IPC and Sections 5/6 of the POCSO Act.
The trial court had sentenced him to death under Sections 376AB and 302 IPC.
It had also imposed a five-year rigorous imprisonment sentence under Section 201 IPC.
The Madhya Pradesh High Court subsequently upheld both the conviction and the death sentence.
Thus, he approached the Supreme Court.
The deceased girl was the daughter of Waris's third wife from her previous marriage.
The High Court found that the prosecution had established that he had sexually assaulted the child.
It relied on the testimony of her mother, medical evidence and DNA evidence.
The post-mortem examination found multiple injuries on the child's body, and the medical panel concluded that she had died due to asphyxiation caused by throttling.
The DNA report showed that male Y chromosomes found on the child's clothes matched the Y chromosome DNA profile of Waris.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Wednesday directed the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) to place on record data on the number of insurance policies issued by public and private sector insurers to persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Intellectual Disability and Multiple Disabilities.

A bench of Justice B.V. Nagarathna and Justice R. Mahadevan passed the order in a PIL which seeks measures to address alleged systemic failures in protecting the rights of persons with neurodevelopmental and other disabilities.

“Learned counsel appearing for the Insurance Regulatory Development Authority(IRDA) to seek instructions by way of presenting the data so far as the number of policies that have been issued by both Public Sector as well as the Private Sector Insurance Companies to insure the life of persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities by the next date of hearing”, the Court ordered.

The petitioner has argued that insurance coverage for autistic persons is effectively non-existent or inadequate despite the regulatory framework requiring insurers to provide coverage to persons with disabilities and mental illness.
During the hearing, counsel for IRDAI referred to circulars issued by the regulator on insurance coverage for persons with disabilities and mental illness.

The Court then asked IRDAI to obtain instructions and present data showing the number of policies issued by both public sector and private sector insurance companies to insure the life of persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Intellectual Disability and Multiple Disabilities.
The information has to be placed before the Court by the next date of hearing on November 19th.

The PIL seeks directions to address "persistent neglect, institutional apathy, and failure" in upholding constitutional, statutory and international obligations towards persons with neurodivergent conditions such as autism, dyslexia and ADHD.

The petition alleges systemic failures in the implementation of the National Trust Act, 1999, the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 and the National Trust (Amendment) Act, 2018.
It states that despite these laws, significant gaps remain in mental health infrastructure, funding, accessibility and public awareness.
The petition points to inadequate budgetary allocations, shortage of rehabilitation centres and inadequate community-based rehabilitation services.
It also alleges that stigma and institutional apathy continue to hinder rehabilitation and social inclusion.

article_sentences: The Court cautioned against automatic arrest in such cases, and directed the invovlement of a child psychiatrist in the investigation.

The Supreme Court today (24 September) has laid down a set of safeguards to prevent the misuse of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO Act) as a weapon in matrimonial and child custody disputes.

The safeguards were laid down while quashing an FIR alleging sexual assault of a minor girl by her father, after a probe by the Central Investigation Agency (CBI) found the allegations to be unreliable.

A bench of Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice KV Viswanathan was dealing with a batch of appeals arising out of a bitter and long-drawn custody battle between a divorced couple, referred to in the judgment as 'R' (father) and 'E' (mother), over their minor daughter 'M'.
The Court has flagged the growing misuse of POCSO Act in matrimonial disputes.

Referring to precedents like Geddam Jhansi v State of Telangana, Achin Gupta v State of Haryana, Ishwar Chand Sharma v State of UP, and Kerala High Court's Suhara v Muhammed Jaleel, the bench noted a worrying trend of spouses filing false POCSO complaints to gain leverage in custody battles or extract better settlements.

The bench observed that while Section 22 of the POCSO Act penalises false complaints, “by the time Section 22 is invoked substantial damage would be caused to the party falsely charged,” in the form of either prolonged incarceration or adverse impact on pending guardianship or custody proceedings.
It therefore held that “certain precautions must be taken, within the four corners of the law, to prevent such harm from befalling the accused.”

“Any precaution we envision to prevent irreparable harm to the accused in certain contexts and circumstances must, therefore, not run counter to the stated object of the Act, or dilute the stringency with which such offences are meant to be treated.

What is needed is a balancing exercise: precautions that neither dilute the object of the Act nor weaken its provisions, while allowing sufficient leeway to ensure that irreparable harm is not caused to the accused,” the bench further clarified.
The bench further clarified that the safeguards would apply only where two threshold conditions are met.
One, an offence under the POCSO Act is alleged to have been committed by a parent or family member living under the same roof as the child victim.

stories.title: India’s market regulator SEBI widens FPI access to commodity derivatives
stories.summary: At its latest Board meeting, SEBI widened foreign portfolio investor access to exchange-traded commodity derivatives, confirming a CNBC-TV18 report earlier this month that the regulator was set to open up more non-agricultural contracts to FPIs.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'market regulator' in title weight 40
article_sentences: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Board, at its meeting on Thursday, approved wider participation by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) in exchange-traded commodity derivatives, allowing them to access a broader set of non-agricultural contracts.
The SEBI Board’s decision confirms a CNBC-TV18 news break from September 4, which reported that the regulator was set to allow FPIs to participate in commodity derivatives.
Sources had told CNBC-TV18 that SEBI was expected to permit FPI trading in non-cash-settled, non-agricultural commodity derivatives, broadly along the lines proposed in its consultation paper.

The market regulator has approved FPI participation in non-agricultural index derivatives, irrespective of whether the underlying contracts are cash-settled, as well as non-cash-settled non-agricultural commodity derivatives.
However, FPIs participating in non-cash-settled non-agricultural commodity derivatives will have to exit their positions before any delivery obligation arises.
Under the new framework, FPIs will have to square off their positions before the start of the Tender Period, which begins three days before the expiry of a contract.
They will also not be allowed to increase their positions from the T-3 day.
If an FPI fails to exit its position, the open position can be transferred to its trading member or trading-cum-clearing member (TM/TCM), subject to the agreed arrangements.

Before an FPI is enabled to trade on an exchange, it will have to enter into an agreement with its TM/TCM specifying how its positions will be handled, including arrangements for squaring off positions ahead of the delivery obligation.
SEBI said the transfer of an FPI’s open position to the TM/TCM will be treated as a trade and will attract applicable statutory levies.
The regulator said the move is aimed at deepening liquidity in the commodity derivatives market, while ensuring that FPIs do not enter the physical delivery process.

The move is expected to benefit commodity exchanges and trading platforms, including Multi Commodity Exchange of India (MCX), BSE and NSE, by potentially broadening participation and liquidity in eligible contracts.
